Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I apologize for the confusion earlier. Mr. Chairman, the United States requested a recorded vote on resolutions A and B and is voting no due to a number of concerns we have with the text. First, the United States will not accept suppression of freedom of expression under the guise of combating disinformation and misinformation. Government censorship of speech is intolerable in a free society, and these terms are tools to police and moderate public debate. The United States is making every effort to protect freedom of expression, and we will not tolerate efforts to trample it at home or abroad. We will not shy away from calling out countries imposing censorship tactics such as government-imposed shutdowns of the internet and undue restrictions on freedom of expression online. We call on other members of states— I'm sorry, other member states to strengthen the free flow of information. Second, we remain vigilant against attempts to inject political or ideological language into United Nations resolutions. This resolution contains numerous references that serve only to shield Beijing from criticisms over its governance systems and human rights abuses. Similarly, the resolutions contain many references to developing countries. We are concerned that countries like China are misappropriating the term to gain advantages in the UN system. We urge the use of more clearly defined terminology that reflects actual national economic conditions. Technical assistance should be based on objective criteria not vague and inconsistent labels. Third, the repeated references to the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the Sustainable Development Goals impinge upon state sovereignty as a soft form of global governance. We no longer reaffirm them as a matter of course. Fourth, in lieu of general references to climate and climate change, UN resolutions should focus on specific environmental threats and sensible environmental protections. Similarly, the references to gender are ambiguous and unclear. The United States expects UN resolutions to use terminology that clearly refers to women and men, girls and boys. Finally, Mr. Chairman, the United States requests whether yearly consideration of these resolutions is a good use of the UN's limited resources. Next year, we look forward to engaging with the Committee on Information to reduce the frequency to once every 2 years and to formulate a more focused, unambiguous, and apolitical report. Thank you, sir.

I have the honor to deliver this explanation of vote on behalf of Australia, New Zealand, and my own country, Canada, in support of the resolutions on information in the service of humanity and the United Nations global communications policies and activities. We wish firstly to express our gratitude to the Secretary-General for his August 2025 report on questions relating to information, to Under-Secretary-General Melissa Fleming for her informative, informative presentation last week, and to the members of the Committee on Information for their diligent, apolitical, and consensus-based work. Chair, these resolutions cover key priorities for CANZ members, including firstly, promoting and protecting human rights, including the right to freedom of opinion and expression and the freedom to seek, receive, and impart information. Secondly, supporting the fulfillment of these rights through efforts to bridge the digital divide protect journalists, advance multilingualism, and foster independent, plural, and diverse media. And finally, engaging in multilateral and whole-of-society efforts to build resilience and counter the threats posed by disinformation, misinformation, and information manipulation. As noted in the Resolution on UN Global Communications Policies and Activities, the safe, secure, and trustworthy use of artificial intelligence has the potential to accelerate progress towards achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. However, AI is also being used for malign purposes, including the creation and spread of disinformation and misinformation, which incites violence, erodes trust in institutions, undermines peace and security, and impedes global cooperation on shared challenges. We welcome the addition of language noting these concerns and reaffirm the importance of multilateral and whole-of-society efforts to safeguard information integrity uphold human rights, and enhance collective resilience.

Mr. Chairman, the members of— we also highlight the new report on the importance of multilingualism in local content. Multilingualism is a linchpin in international relations and diplomacy, specifically here at the United Nations. It reflects the diversity of member states and helps each member state to better express themselves and to better understand the views of others by building our capacity to build a shared future. Moreover, multilingualism is critical for communicating with an international public and for the guarantee of integrity of information. In this regard, we wish to take this opportunity to thank the Department of Global Communications of the United Nations for its significant efforts in the advancement of linguistic diversity while highlighting its key role as a credible source of credible, credible, impartial, and objective information. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. For the Russian Federation, we voted in support of the resolution of the committee— the DGC. We believe that the provisions therein, as they presently stand on the whole, reflect the mandate of the committee and set out key guidelines of the work of the DGC and highlight the importance of multilingualism, objectivity, and impartiality in the official information resources of the UN, as well as the need to build the capability of our organization in the area of global communications. At the same time, it is with regret that we have to note that the document which over many years was adopted by consensus, which was viewed by member states as a unifying foundation for work on information, this year was put to the vote. The text of the resolution was drafted during open, inclusive, and rather complicated consultations with the participation of the G77 G7 plus China, the European Union, and a broad range of delegations. As a result of this work, agreement was reached on balanced language— language reflecting the contribution of all participants, which of course allowed for us to hope that consensus-based practice would be maintained. We believe that the agreements arrived at at the committee need to be honored and not revised unilaterally at the final stage following the completion of negotiations. A departure from existing consensus-based tradition on such a sensitive and at the same time consolidating issue is a step which does not help to build trust among member states and does not help to enhance the effectiveness of work on the information-related agenda. At the same time, we stress that today's vote does not diminish the importance of the resolution and the parameters for the DGC: multilingualism, equal access to information, and transparency in activities of the United Nations. We are keen to see this document continue to serve as a guide for the Secretariat and Member States. We trust that during preparations for the next resolution, all delegations will constructively and ahead of time join negotiations, and the Fourth Committee will revert back to the process of consensus-based adoption of this important document reflecting the shared, not divisive, agenda in the sphere of global communications. Thank you for your attention.
